What if the Honda e Returned to the Car World as an Electric Pickup?
12 photos
Photo: Behance | Mahan Rasouli
The Honda e may no longer be a thing, as the Japanese company pulled the plug on it almost three years ago, but that hasn’t stopped a rendering artist from imagining it as a pickup.
That’s right, you did not really think that the automaker actually revived this nameplate, and instead of a hatchback, it decided to launch a workhorse, did you? Yeah, that would be a no. As for the pixel master behind this project, he is Mahan Rasouli, and he recently took to Behance to drop these digital illustrations.
A side-by-side comparison reveals the differences between the real Honda e and this rendered pickup. However, between us, there was no need for such a thing, because the changes are more than visible. After all, the workhorse has room for only two inside. It also has a significantly shorter roofline, which was cut behind the B-pillars, and these are now a lot thicker, as you can clearly see.
Further back, the workhorse project sports redesigned rear three-quarter panels, which may follow the styling of the ones on the real thing, but they were adapted to fit the vehicle’s new body style. The tailgate opens up into the cargo area, and the pixel artist says that this thing would have around 500 liters (cubic feet) of usable storage volume. It would also be 3.5 percent longer, 1.0 percent wider, and 2.6 percent taller compared to the real Honda e.
Photo: Behance | Mahan Rasouli Nothing else has changed, by the looks of it, as the front fascia carries over with no mods. This includes the round headlights, the closed-off grille, and the bumper. The front hood is also the same, and the side cameras instead of the traditional door mirrors also soldier on from the defunct electric hatchback . The shape of the taillights, the trim in the middle of the tailgate, and the rear bumper are also the same.
Even the wheels have been retained, though from what we can see, they are a tiny bit smaller on the rendered electric pickup, and they appear to have been shod in slightly thicker rubber. We should also mention the new wheel arch trim, which is black, for a more utilitarian look, and the fact that this machine has a slightly higher ground clearance compared to the EV hatch on which it builds.
And the interior is also the same , by the way, to no one’s surprise, save for the obvious two-seat layout. The dashboard panel consists of three main screens, including the infotainment system, the display in front of the passenger, and the digital gauge cluster behind the two-spoke, multi-function steering wheel. These are flanked by two more screens, which are directly tied to the side cameras that have replaced the traditional door mirrors.
Honda’s e was on the quite futuristic side of things, both inside and out, and to be honest, it did not look half bad. In fact, it was very cute overall, but that wasn’t enough to save it from the chopping block. The company pulled the plug on it in January 2024, blaming the decision on poor sales. Production started toward the end of 2020 at the Yorii factory in Saitama, Japan, and this model was a subcompact electric hatchback, or a supermini if you will.
Photo: Behance | Mahan Rasouli It featured a rear-motor and rear-wheel drive layout, and came with a pair of electric powertrain options, which were rated at 134 hp (136 ps/100 kW ) and 152 hp (154 ps/113 kW), both having 232 pound-feet (315 Nm) of torque. Honda said 0-62 mph (0 to 100 kph) took over 8 seconds, and a Sport driving mode was on deck to sharpen things up. The car could also be driven in the Single Pedal Control mode, and had a range of around 140 miles (220 km) with the 35.5 kWh lithium-ion battery pack fully charged.
The retro styling and the mix of design and functionality have granted it extra points, but the limited range and the high price were the last nails in its coffin. Before it drove off into the sunset, the 154 ps Honda e Advance version was listed on the company’s UK website from 37,395 pounds, and that’s $49,500 at today’s exchange rate. By comparison, the MINI Electric was offered from 32,550 GBP ($43,085), and the Fiat 500 EV from 28,195 ($37,325).
In case you forgot, Honda never sold the e in the United States of America, because it was considered that the small EV segment and the poor autonomy would not be suitable for our market. It was, however, marketed in Europe, and, as we already told you, it did not do too well for itself, so the brand ended up pulling the plug on it almost two years ago.
Do you miss the Honda e? And if you do, what’s your take on this rendered Honda e Pickup?
